video_notes.title: How to Systematically Setup LLM Evals (Metrics, Unit Tests, LLM-as-a-Judge)
video_notes.contributed: Lays out the three-level eval ladder (unit tests -> human/LLM judge -> AB testing) and a concrete Excel-based judge-alignment workflow with an agreement-score metric; closest thing here to a 'build' process, but for evals, not fine-tuning.

video_notes.title: The Never Ending Lore of Harness | Vivek Trivedy (Product Lead, Langchain)
video_notes.contributed: Defines harness engineering (model + harness), gives concrete context-budget numbers for sub-agents, and frames explicitly when to reach for RL/fine-tuning on an open model versus when to stay with harness/context engineering.

video_notes.title: GenAI in Production: How AI Is Transforming the Entire Filmmaking Pipeline
video_notes.contributed: Only video in the cluster describing an actual fine-tuning use case in production: LoRA-based digital doubles and Gaussian-splat environment capture inside a VFX pipeline, plus real client cost/control tradeoffs.

video_notes.title: The challenges in using LLM-as-a-Judge - Sourabh Agrawal | Vector Space Talk #013
video_notes.contributed: Covers the economics and engineering of LLM-as-judge systems: cheap models for scale, root-cause analysis on failing slices, objective fact-level scoring, and dataset sizing (50-100 samples).

claims.theme: Industry failure rate of agent projects
claims.claim: Gartner and MIT reports cited predict 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by 2027, and MIT found 95% of generative AI pilots are failing -- used to motivate why evals matter.
claims.quote: 40% of all agent AI projects is expected to be cancelled

claims.claim: Evals can be run as background monitoring, as real-time guardrails that block bad outputs, or as improvement tools that label data for fine-tuning or custom test sets.
claims.quote: label data for either fine-tuning

claims.claim: Apply an iterative analyze -> measure -> improve lifecycle (collect/categorize failures, turn them into quantitative metrics, then refine prompts/models/architecture) as the operating loop for improving an LLM system.
claims.quote: analyze, measure, improve life cycle

claims.claim: Evals split into three escalating levels -- unit tests (level 1), human-and-model evaluation (level 2), and AB testing (level 3) -- with cost and effort increasing at each level.
claims.quote: we get to human and model evaluation

claims.claim: The simplest LLM unit test checks structured-output fields directly: assert the predicted category is in the allowed category list, confidence is a float between 0 and 1, and category equals the expected value for a known input.
claims.quote: check whether the category is in all of the categories

claims.claim: Run unit tests on every code/prompt change, run human-and-model evals weekly or bi-weekly depending on system complexity, and reserve AB testing for major releases.
claims.quote: you want to run these weekly or bi-weekly

claims.claim: When moving to LLM-as-a-judge, use the most powerful model you can afford (e.g. GPT-4.1 or Claude Sonnet class) rather than a cheap mini model, because the judge's reasoning quality has to be trusted.
claims.quote: use the most powerful model that you can afford

claims.theme: Judge should explain, not just score
claims.claim: A good LLM judge produces a detailed critique explaining its reasoning, not just a bare score -- the explanation is what lets you diagnose and later align the judge.
claims.quote: detailed critiques, not just scores

claims.claim: To build an aligned evaluator: collect model predictions, generate model critiques, get human evaluations on the same data, compare model versus human judgments, iterate on the evaluator prompt, and repeat until agreement is high.
claims.quote: you collect model predictions, you generate model critiques

claims.claim: In a 10-example worked example comparing human labels to model-judge labels side by side in a spreadsheet, the human/model agreement score came out to 70% on the first pass.
claims.quote: a 70% agreement score

claims.claim: Export the disagreement cases (input, output, human critique, model critique) and feed them to a strong model as a meta-prompt asking it to rewrite the judge prompt to close the gap -- then re-run and check if agreement rises.
claims.quote: you could then create a metaprompt

claims.claim: Reaching for a new tool (vector DB, bigger model, eval platform) before understanding the actual failure is the first common eval mistake; fix is to start simple and build custom solutions based on what you actually need.
claims.quote: the first one is tool first thinking

claims.claim: Drowning in generic scores like 'helpfulness 4.2, truthfulness 4.5' tells you nothing actionable; fix is to start with specific boolean metrics tied to what you actually want to know.
claims.quote: mistake number two, generic metrics obsessions

claims.claim: A principal engineer at Zapier reportedly spends three hours per day looking at traces and raw data -- cited as proof that manual data inspection is irreplaceable even for senior engineers.
claims.quote: spends three hours per day looking at traces

claims.claim: Shipping an LLM judge without first validating it against human judgment is a core mistake; always validate judge alignment with a human in the loop before trusting its scores.
claims.quote: mistake number four is unaligned LLM judges

claims.claim: Reference-based metrics (exact string match, semantic similarity, code execution results, SQL correctness, structured-data validation) are easier to automate because you know the golden answer; most real systems also need reference-free metrics like tone and hallucination checks.
claims.quote: exact string matching, semantic similarity, code execution results

claims.claim: An agent is best defined as model plus harness, where a harness is every piece of code, configuration, or execution logic that is not the model itself -- giving teams shared language for what to optimize.
claims.quote: every piece of code, configuration, or execution logic

claims.claim: Prompting is the first pillar of a good harness and covers more than the system prompt -- it includes tool descriptions, skill front matter, and sub-agent front matter that specify when and how each should be used.
claims.quote: prompting and like very very clear instructions

claims.claim: Agents are susceptible to picking the easy way out in self-verification -- testing trivial cases instead of hard ones -- so harnesses must explicitly teach agents to be thorough when verifying their own work.
claims.quote: picking the easy way out in verification

claims.claim: Size sub-agent tasks to roughly a 50k-150k (up to ~200k depending on model) token working range -- big enough to be useful, small enough to avoid the 'dumb zone' from context rot.
claims.quote: a 50k to like a 150k token range

claims.theme: More reasoning effort can hurt under time limits
claims.claim: On a time-bounded terminal-bench style run, using X-high reasoning end-to-end scored only 53.9% (due to timeouts) versus 63.6% when execution used high effort -- more reasoning is not free when the task has a hard time budget.
claims.quote: scored 53.9% due to timeouts versus 63.6% at high

claims.theme: File system as foundational harness primitive
claims.claim: The file system is described as arguably the most foundational harness primitive: models are already very good at using it, and it gives agents persistent storage to both pull context in and offload it, including as a shared scratchpad across sub-agents.
claims.quote: the file system is arguably the most foundational harness primitive

claims.theme: When to reach for RL / fine-tuning
claims.claim: RL/fine-tuning is worth it when you have curated vertical data and want a model that's both much better and much cheaper/faster at that one task -- e.g. fine-tuning on customer-service or finance data to beat a general model at that niche.
claims.quote: fine-tune on a bunch of our like customer service data

claims.theme: Fine-tuned open model can beat a closed model
claims.claim: Depending on how well a task is represented in a frontier lab's training mixture, a fine-tuned open model built on your own data is very likely to outperform an unfine-tuned closed model on that specific task.
claims.quote: your fine-tuned model will be better than that open model

claims.theme: Start with harness engineering before RL
claims.claim: Before investing in RL/fine-tuning, it's a really good idea to start with harness engineering (or plain context engineering) because it's cheap relative to RL -- build a simple harness around the base model first and only escalate once that's insufficient.
claims.quote: a really good idea just to start with harness engineering

claims.claim: The main levers against context rot are sub-agent decomposition, compaction, tool-call offloading, and skills with progressive disclosure -- these are typically used in combination, not alone.
claims.quote: compaction, tool call offloading, skills

claims.claim: For noisy tool output (e.g. a giant bash/shell result), pipe only the head and tail into the model's context and tell it the full string lives in a file it can read later if needed, instead of dumping everything into context.
claims.quote: take like the head and the tail

claims.claim: Beyond pass/fail, track fine-grained eval metrics like total time taken, number of tokens used, and overall cost, plus reading the trajectory itself to see whether context-rot mitigations are actually working.
claims.quote: how many tokens did it take

claims.claim: Open models like the GLM series surprised the team this year as genuinely good, fast agentic coding partners -- a credible base for teams who want to fine-tune rather than depend solely on frontier closed models.
claims.quote: the GLM series is like fantastic

claims.claim: Hooks (middleware) that inject deterministic code execution into the harness -- e.g. forcing self-verification before an agent is allowed to exit -- are an underrated, high-leverage harness feature most teams underuse.
claims.quote: we call it middleware but like hooks

claims.theme: Evals as the grounding signal for self-improvement
claims.claim: Evals function as the grounding mechanism for auto-research / meta-harness self-improvement loops -- they let you hill-climb a harness over time because the same measurement still applies weeks later, not just in the moment.
claims.quote: evals are basically how we like ground our

claims.claim: As agents do longer-horizon work, evals are shifting away from simple input/output chat-completion checks toward full task environments the agent is dropped into and evaluated within (e.g. via Harbor/terminal-bench style setups).
claims.quote: evals are going to start looking like environments

claims.claim: Public benchmarks are only a rough vibe-check; the real lever for improving an agent is building your own representative bench of evals/tasks tagged to axes (retrieval, planning, tool use) that map to your actual product.
claims.quote: get a representative set of like evals and tasks like my own bench

claims.claim: The general-purpose recipe for longer-horizon agent tasks is: decompose the hard problem into sub-pieces, then verify each intermediate step so mistakes are caught and fixed before they compound.
claims.quote: decomposing a really difficult problem into like sub pieces

claims.claim: Promise's Generation Company fine-tunes models per actor -- e.g. creating a LoRA to build a digital double -- rather than relying purely on prompting a general model, blending that with traditional VFX methods depending on the use case.
claims.quote: we will create like things like a Laura

claims.claim: To recreate decades-old crime-scene environments from low-resolution archival photos, the team generated images with GenAI and then used them to build a Gaussian-splat 3D representation of the environment for display on a 16K LED wall.
claims.quote: create a gauzing splat three-dimensional representation of that environment

claims.claim: Client budget sits on a pendulum: swing toward fast-and-cheap GenAI output and you get what you get with less control; swing toward traditional VFX/comp work layered on top and you buy back control, asset-by-asset.
claims.quote: there's a pendulum, right? And it could swing

claims.claim: Commercial GenAI tools (e.g. Freepik, Luma) are rated about an 8 out of 10 for consistency/control, but traditional VFX is still required to bring shots to broadcast quality.
claims.quote: Yeah, it's like an eight out of 10

claims.claim: Paranormal Activity cost roughly half a million dollars to make and grossed roughly a billion dollars over its lifetime, cited as the budget-efficiency model GenAI filmmaking should chase instead of $1.5B-breakeven tentpoles.
claims.quote: cost like half a million dollars

claims.claim: Every generated image is run through a proprietary 'Copyright Guardian' check that flags elements (e.g. a background painting) that are too similar to copyrighted work before anything can be published or distributed.
claims.quote: every single image we gener generate through copyright guardian

claims.claim: To be able to distribute through studios like Paramount, Promise maintains enterprise deals with all of its model makers so chain-of-title, data security, and indemnification requirements are met before any model is used in production.
claims.quote: we have enterprise deals with all of our models

claims.theme: Embedding GenAI artists in production departments
claims.claim: A concrete service model: embed a GenAI artist directly inside a studio's art/costume/props/wardrobe department working side-by-side with the department head so ideas get visualized and iterated faster.
claims.quote: we can embed an artist directly into the studio

claims.claim: For the CBS Paramount true-crime series 'Harlan Coben's Final Twist', the team produced over 400 fully generated shots used as additional B-roll across five episodes.
claims.quote: we worked on over 400 fully generated shots

claims.theme: Don't use an expensive model as judge
claims.claim: Avoid using an expensive frontier model like GPT-4 purely for evaluation at scale -- if you're spending more on judging than generating, you might as well have a human do it; rely on smaller, cheaper models for most checks.
claims.quote: you don't want to use like an expensive model like gp4

claims.claim: Don't run every check on every data point; run a high-level check across all traffic, then on the 10-20% of cases that fail, run a battery of 5-10 deeper checks to pinpoint whether the failure is retrieval, citation, utilization, or hallucination.
claims.quote: run like a a battery of checks on them

claims.claim: Instead of asking an LLM judge for a subjective relevant/irrelevant or Likert rating (which invites egocentric bias), break the response into individual facts and score each fact's relevance, then aggregate into a ratio-based score.
claims.quote: break down the response into like individual facts

claims.claim: For any RAG application, start evaluation with four or five metrics: response relevance, response completeness, context relevance (retrieval quality), hallucination/groundedness, and conversation satisfaction -- optionally tonality if it matters.
claims.quote: look at the relevance of the response

claims.claim: A test dataset of just 50-100 samples drawn from real user traffic (or downvoted/failed responses) is a good enough starting point for evaluation -- it beats synthetic data or public benchmarks, which can't anticipate your real issues.
claims.quote: a test data sets of like 50 to 100 samples

claims.theme: Real-time eval limited to latency-tolerant checks
claims.claim: Most quality evals (relevance, hallucination) can't run before the response is shown to the user because checking adds latency; only safety/jailbreak checks are cheap enough to run in parallel with generation.
claims.quote: checking requires extra time and you don't want to add latency

claims.claim: Jailbreak attempts tend to show up as abnormally long prompts, bursts of repeated traffic (multiple techniques tried in quick succession), and lower sentiment/coherence than genuine questions.
claims.quote: the length of their question or the length of their prompt

claims.claim: UpTrain's core workflow is a single API call -- log and evaluate -- where you pass question/response/context plus the checks you want (context relevance, completeness, jailbreak, safety, satisfaction) and get back a score with an explanation.
claims.quote: up train. log and evaluate

claims.claim: UpTrain can filter down to all cases that scored zero on a given check and automatically surface the common topic across them, turning a pile of failures into an actionable pattern to fix.
claims.quote: filter cases where let's say the model is failing

claims.claim: Run side-by-side experiments comparing two models or prompts (e.g. GPT-3.5 vs Claude 2) across multiple metrics at once, then decide which metric matters most for your users before picking a winner.
claims.quote: compare like two different models right so GPD 3.5 and Claw 2

disagreements.topic: What model to use as an LLM judge

positions.position: Use the most powerful model you can afford for LLM-as-a-judge (GPT-4.1 / Claude Sonnet class) -- this is explicitly not a job for mini/cheap models.
Avoid using an expensive model like GPT-4 for evaluation at scale; rely on smaller, cheaper models, because judging cost otherwise outweighs the value and you'd be better off with a human.

gaps: None of the four videos actually walk through how to fine-tune a model: no data-format prep, no training script, no hyperparameters (learning rate, epochs, LoRA rank/alpha), no infra/tooling choice (e.g. axolotl, Unsloth, TRL), and no cost or wall-clock-time figures for running a fine-tune.
NovNcsKX8AU references fine-tuning open models (GLM-5, Kimi) and doing RL on trace data, but gives no concrete recipe for turning traces into training data or running the RL job itself.

NRQVTxl14x8 mentions creating a LoRA for a digital double but gives no detail on the training process, dataset size, or tooling used to produce it -- that work is attributed to a separate 'Muse' team not covered in the talk.

None of the talks compare fine-tuning against prompting/RAG on cost or quality for a concrete task, so a reader can't tell from this cluster when fine-tuning actually beats a well-engineered harness or eval-driven prompt loop.

No discussion of evaluating a fine-tuned model specifically (e.g. catastrophic forgetting, regression suites for a fine-tuned checkpoint) distinct from the general LLM-eval guidance given for prompted systems.
No treatment of fine-tuning for safety/alignment, or of open-weight licensing/legal constraints on fine-tuning, despite NRQVTxl14x8's heavy focus on copyright/chain-of-title for generated images.
